Question: What is COPD life expectancy?

message.content:
**There is no single life expectancy for COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).** It can shorten life, particularly when airflow obstruction is severe, but a diagnosis or “stage” alone cannot tell you how many years you have left. The outlook also depends on smoking, breathlessness, oxygen levels, flare-ups, physical fitness and other health conditions. [NICE guidance](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542426/)

### What do the numbers show?

A study published in 2026 pooled **45,886 people from eight US studies**. Its age-adjusted model estimated the following **average years of life remaining at age 65**—not years remaining from diagnosis. [JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2848783)

| Degree of airflow obstruction | Estimated years remaining at age 65 |
|---|---:|
| No COPD | 21.5 years |
| GOLD stage 1 | 20.0 years |
| GOLD stage 2 | 16.4 years |
| GOLD stage 3 | 13.1 years |
| GOLD stage 4 | 10.7 years |

These figures are **population estimates, not a personal countdown**. The study defined COPD using breathing tests taken before an airway-opening medicine, and its participants were followed through 2020. Its stage 4 estimate, for example, had a 95% confidence interval of 8.9–12.6 years—reflecting uncertainty in the estimated average, not the range of survival for individual people. [JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2848783)

### What matters for your own outlook?

A clinician should look beyond the stage and consider:
- Your breathing-test results, including **FEV₁**—how much air you can force out in one second.
- Whether you still smoke.
- How often you have flare-ups or need hospital treatment.
- Your oxygen levels, breathlessness and ability to exercise.
- Low body weight, frailty and other illnesses. [NICE guidance](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542426/)

### What can you do?

**If you smoke, quitting is the most effective way to prevent COPD getting worse**, even in advanced disease. Treatment cannot cure COPD, but can help slow its progression and control symptoms. Inhalers can ease breathing, and pulmonary rehabilitation—an exercise and education programme—can improve exercise tolerance and symptoms. [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/chronic-obstructive-pulmonary-disease-copd/treatment/)

For people with persistently low oxygen levels who meet the criteria, prescribed long-term oxygen therapy can improve survival; it is not needed by everyone with COPD. [NICE](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs10/resources/chronic-obstructive-pulmonary-disease-in-adults-pdf-2098478592709)

**The most useful next step:** ask your clinician, “Given my lung function, oxygen levels and recent flare-ups, what is my likely outlook—and what can we do to improve it?”

url_citation.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) - Treatment
url_citation.content:
There's currently no cure for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), but treatment can help slow the progression of the condition and control the symptoms.

...

Treatments include:

...

- stopping smoking – if you have COPD and you smoke, this is the most important thing you can do
- inhalers and tablets – to help make breathing easier
- pulmonary rehabilitation – a specialised programme of exercise and education
- surgery or a lung transplant – although this is only an option for a very small number of people

...

A doctor will discuss the various treatment options with you.

...

## Stop smoking

...

If you smoke, stopping is the most effective way to prevent COPD getting worse.

Although any damage done to your lungs and airways cannot be reversed, giving up smoking can help prevent further damage.

...

This may be all the treatment that's needed in the early stages of COPD, but it's never too late to stop – even people with more advanced COPD will benefit from quitting.

...

If you think you need help to stop smoking, visit Quit smoking for free advice and support.

...

## Pulmonary rehabilitation

...

Pulmonary rehabilitation is a specialised programme of exercise and education designed to help people with lung problems such as COPD.

It can help improve how much exercise you're able to do before you feel out of breath, as well as your symptoms, self-confidence and emotional wellbeing.

...

Pulmonary rehabilitation programmes usually involve 2 or more group sessions a week for at least 6 weeks.

A typical programme includes:

...

- physical exercise training tailored to your needs and ability – such as walking, cycling and strength exercises
- education about your condition for you and your family
- dietary advice
- psychological and emotional support

...

The programmes are provided by a number of different healthcare professionals, including physiotherapists, nurse specialists and dietitians.

...

### Long-term oxygen therapy

...

If COPD causes a low level of oxygen in your blood, you may be advised to have oxygen at home through nasal tubes or a mask.

This can help stop the level of oxygen in your blood becoming dangerously low, although it's not a treatment for the main symptoms of COPD, such as breathlessness.

...

Long-term oxygen treatment should be used for at least 15 hours a day.

...

The tubes from the machine are long, so you will be able to move around your home while you're connected. Portable oxygen tanks are available if you need to use oxygen away from home.

...

Do not smoke when using oxygen. The increased level of oxygen is highly flammable and a lit cigarette could cause a fire or explosion.

...

Some people with COPD will benefit from ambulatory oxygen, which is oxygen you use when you walk or are active in other ways.

...

If your blood oxygen levels are normal while you're resting but fall when you exercise, you may be able to have ambulatory oxygen therapy rather than long-term oxygen therapy.

Question: What is COPD life expectancy?

message.content:
**Short answer:** There isn't one life expectancy for COPD. It depends mostly on how severe your airflow blockage is and whether you smoke. Mild COPD may shorten life very little. Severe COPD can shorten it by about 5 to 9 years. Studies report averages, and they can't predict what will happen to one person.

**Large US study (45,886 people, 8 cohorts)**
- Researchers compared people with COPD to people with no airflow obstruction. They looked at years of life lost (YLL) by GOLD stage, which grades severity from 1 (mild) to 4 (very severe). The YLL were about 0.7 years for stage 1, 2.6 for stage 2, 5.1 for stage 3, and 7.1 for stage 4. [JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2848783)
- For a 65-year-old, average remaining life expectancy was 21.5 years without COPD. It was 20.0 years for stage 1, 16.4 for stage 2, 13.1 for stage 3, and 10.7 for stage 4. [JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2848783)
- The study reported similar decreases in people who never smoked and in people who had smoked. [JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2848783)
- The estimates were adjusted for factors including smoking, body mass index, diabetes and hypertension. [JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2848783)

**Older US study (NHANES III follow-up)**
- This study found smoking status mattered a lot. COPD reduced life expectancy only modestly in never-smokers but very substantially in current and former smokers. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19436692/)
- At age 65, men who were current smokers lost 0.3 years with stage 1 COPD, 2.2 years with stage 2, and 5.8 years with stage 3 or 4. These losses are on top of 3.5 years lost to smoking itself. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19436692/)
- Male never-smokers lost 0.7 years (stage 2) and 1.3 years (stage 3 or 4). [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2672796/)
- This study's results differ from the JAMA study, which found similar losses regardless of smoking history. The two used different cohorts and methods, so the findings don't fully agree.

**Other estimates**
- A hospital study in Taiwan (532 patients) estimated about 9 years of life lost for GOLD stage 3–4 COPD. It found about 6 years lost for stage 2 and no measurable loss for stage 1. People who had been hospitalized for a severe flare-up (exacerbation) in the prior year had a similar loss of about 8–9 years. [ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0954611120302729)
- Survival figures from a small prospective study of 170 patients were 62% at 5 years and 35% at 10 years. [MDPI Diagnostics](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4418/13/7/1344) A pooled analysis of 3,633 patients from 11 cohorts found survival of 43% at 10 years. [COCOMICS study summary](https://exa.ai/library/publication/qjvsq6f3947) These groups were mixed and often included people with more advanced disease, so don't treat them as typical for everyone with COPD.

**What shapes an individual's outlook**
- Airflow obstruction (GOLD stage) is only one factor. The BODE index also takes in body weight (BMI), breathlessness, and how far you can walk in six minutes. It predicted death risk better than airflow alone. [NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa021322)
- In that NEJM study, most deaths were from respiratory failure (61%), and the rest were mainly heart attack (14%) and lung cancer (12%). [NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa021322)
- Other studies compared scoring systems that add age and flare-ups. None predicts short-term survival well. [COCOMICS study summary](https://exa.ai/library/publication/qjvsq6f3947)

**Caveats**
- These are averages from past groups of people. The cohorts began years ago, so they may not reflect current treatment.
- The sources I found don't show how much quitting smoking, medicines, rehabilitation or vaccines change these numbers. The older US study did say its findings were "further reason for smokers to quit." [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19436692/)

Ask your doctor about your own stage and risk score. They can give you a more personal estimate than these averages can.

## Highlights
* •Few studies directly address the question of life expectancy (LE) and loss of LEfor severe stage COPD.
* •The loss-of-LE of severe stage COPD patients is almost the same as those with one or more severe AE history, or, 8-9 years.
* •73.8% of COPD patients were under diagnosed.
* •Patients who were never made a diagnosis of COPD before their first time ofsevere AE had a loss-of-LE of 9.8 years.
## Abstract
### Background and objectives
Prognosis of COPD is usually expressed as a 3-year survival rate, which might not be easily understood by lay people. This study estimates the life expectancy (LE) and loss-of-LE for COPD patients with different GOLD stages and patients with a history of acute exacerbation (AE) requiring hospitalization (severe AE) in the preceding year.
### Methods
532 patients who were diagnosed with COPD according to the GOLD criteria at NCKU hospital between 2006 and 2016 were recruited. Survival was estimated by Kaplan-Meier method, and extrapolated to lifetime to obtain the LE. The loss-of-LE was quantified by subtracting the LE of the COPD cohort from national life tables. The survival of patients with severe AE history was validated by a nation-wide cohort from the National Health Insurance dataset.
### Results
The survival of patients with severe stage COPD (GOLD grades 3 and 4) was almost the same as those patients with a history of severe AE and the loss-of-LE for the former and the latter were 9.3 (1.1) and 9.4 (1.3) years, respectively. The nation-wide cohort with severe AE history (n=44,764) showed a loss-of-LE of 8.3 (0.1) years. The loss-of-LE of patients with moderate stage COPD (GOLD grade 2) was 6.2 years, but no reduction in LE was noted for mild stage COPD (GOLD grade 1).
### Conclusions
We successfully estimated LE and loss of LE in COPD patients under the GOLD criteria. The survival of severe stage COPD patients is almost the same as those with severe AE history, or about 8–9 years of life lost.

## Abstract
### Background
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by an incompletely reversible limitation in airflow. A physiological variable —the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) —is often used to grade the severity of COPD. However, patients with COPD have systemic manifestations that are not reflected by the FEV1. We hypothesized that a multidimensional grading system that assessed the respiratory and systemic expressions of COPD would better categorize and predict outcome in these patients.
### Methods
We first evaluated 207 patients and found that four factors predicted the risk of death in this cohort: the body-mass index (B), the degree of airflow obstruction (O) and dyspnea (D), and exercise capacity (E), measured by the six-minute–walk test. We used these variables to construct the BODE index, a multidimensional 10-point scale in which higher scores indicate a higher risk of death. We then prospectively validated the index in a cohort of 625 patients, with death from any cause and from respiratory causes as the outcome variables.
### Results
There were 25 deaths among the first 207 patients and 162 deaths (26 percent) in the validation cohort. Sixty-one percent of the deaths in the validation cohort were due to respiratory insufficiency, 14 percent to myocardial infarction, 12 percent to lung cancer, and 13 percent to other causes. Patients with higher BODE scores were at higher risk for death; the hazard ratio for death from any cause per one-point increase in the BODE score was 1.34 (95 percent confidence interval, 1.26 to 1.42; P<0.001), and the hazard ratio for death from respiratory causes was 1.62 (95 percent confidence interval, 1.48 to 1.77; P<0.001). The C statistic for the ability of the BODE index to predict the risk of death was larger than that for the FEV1(0.74 vs. 0.65).
### Conclusions
The BODE index, a simple multidimensional grading system, is better than the FEV1at predicting the risk of death from any cause and from respiratory causes among patients with COPD.

url_citation.content: Guidelines recommend defining chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) by airflow obstruction and other factors, but no studies have evaluated the ability of existing multicomponent indices to predict mortality up to 10 years. We conducted a patient-based pooled analysis. The ADO and BODE indices are overall the most valid multicomponent indices to predict time to death in all COPD patients.

Question: Who is at high risk for nasopharyngeal cancer?

message.content:
People at higher risk for **nasopharyngeal cancer** include the following groups:

- **People who live in—or have ancestry from—regions where it is more common:** particularly southern China and parts of Southeast Asia, North Africa, and the Arctic. Risk varies within these regions; not everyone of Asian ancestry has the same risk. ([National Cancer Institute](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq), [American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/nasopharyngeal-cancer/causes-risks-prevention.html))
- **People with a family history of nasopharyngeal cancer.** It is unclear how much of this increased risk comes from inherited genes versus shared environmental exposures, such as diet. ([American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/nasopharyngeal-cancer/causes-risks-prevention.html))
- **People infected with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).** EBV is strongly linked to certain types of nasopharyngeal cancer. However, EBV infection is very common, and **infection alone is not enough to cause this cancer**—most infected people never develop it. ([American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/nasopharyngeal-cancer/causes-risks-prevention.html))
- **People who frequently eat salt-cured fish or meats, especially from an early age.** Diets high in these foods are linked to increased risk; this does not mean all salty foods carry the same risk. ([American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/nasopharyngeal-cancer/causes-risks-prevention.html))
- **People who use tobacco, breathe secondhand smoke, or drink alcohol frequently and heavily.** The National Cancer Institute lists these as risk factors; its professional guidance specifically identifies smoking and heavy alcohol intake as risk factors for the *keratinizing* subtype. ([NCI patient guidance](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq), [NCI professional guidance](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/hp/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq))
- **Men**, who develop it more often than women. **Age also matters:** in regions where the cancer is uncommon, it is more often diagnosed after age 50; in high-risk regions, younger people are more likely to be affected. It can occur at any age. ([National Cancer Institute](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq))

Having a risk factor means your chance is higher—not that you will develop the disease. If you have a family history or several of these factors, discuss your individual risk with a healthcare professional. ([National Cancer Institute](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq))

Some of the risk factors for nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) include:

...

Epstein-Barr virus infection (mononucleosis/mono)

...

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection has been linked to the development of NPC, as well as certain lymphomas. It is often found in the non-keratinizing, undifferentiated type of NPC.

...

Infection with EBV is very common throughout the world, often happening in children. In the United States, where infection with this virus tends to occur in teens, it's commonly known as mononucleosis or mono.

...

Infection with EBV alone isn’t enough to cause nasopharyngeal cancer, because infection with this virus is very common and this cancer is very rare. Other factors, such as a person’s genes or smoking, may affect how the body deals with EBV, which may in turn affect how EBV plays a part in the development of nasopharyngeal cancer.

...

Eating certain foods

...

Eating a diet high in salt-cured fish and meat seems to increase the ability of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) to cause nasopharyngeal cancer. Studies show that foods preserved in this way may produce chemicals that can damage DNA. The damaged DNA then changes a cell’s ability to control its growth and reproduction.

In contrast, some studies have suggested that diets high in nuts, legumes, fruits, and vegetables and low in dairy products and meat may help lower the risk of NPC.

...

People who live in parts of Asia, northern Africa, and the Arctic region where NPC is common typically eat diets very high in salt-cured fish and meat starting at an early age. The process of cooking the salted food seems to create chemicals, such as nitrosamine, which is a probable carcinogen.

...

The rate of this cancer is dropping in southeast China and Singapore. This might be partly due to people eating less salt-cured fish.

...

Inherited factors

...

Family members of people with NPC are more likely to get this cancer. It's not known if this is because of inherited genes, shared environmental factors such as the same diet or living quarters, or some combination of these.

...

In areas of the world where nasopharyngeal cancer is not common, older age is a risk factor. In places where NPC is more common, this cancer tends to be seen in younger people.

...

Race, ethnicity, and where you live

...

NPC is most common in Asia, specifically Singapore, Vietnam, the Philippines, and eastern and southern China, including Hong Kong. It is also common in parts of North Africa and the Middle East, as well as the Arctic.

People born in south China have a lower risk of NPC if they move to a part of the world with lower rates of the disease, such as the US or Japan. However, their risk of NPC is still higher than that of people who are native to lower-risk regions. Over time, this risk seems to go down. The risk also goes down in new generations.

...

Although White people born in the United States have a low risk of NPC, White people born in China have a higher risk.

...

Many studies have found that smoking may contribute to the development of nasopharyngeal cancer. Smoking might increase the risk of NPC by reactivating an Epstein-Barr virus infection.

...

Diets high in salt-cured fish have been linked with NPC risk. Avoiding or eating less of this type of food may lower that risk. This is especially true in parts of the world where NPC is common, such as southern China, northern Africa, and the Arctic region.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is one of the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated malignancies and has a characterized geographical distribution (1). In southern China, it is one of the major causes of morbidity and mortality. Despite the heavy public-health burden of NPC in southern China and other endemic areas, relatively little is known about the etiology and prevention of NPC. Although certain environmental exposures, including high consumption of salt-preserved fish, tobacco smoking and lack of fresh fruit and vegetable intake, are generally well accepted as NPC risk factors. To date there has been no rigorous population-based case-control study of NPC in southern China.

...

Since the malignancy was firstly reported in 1901 (8), the etiology of NPC has remained a puzzle for more than a century. Migrant studies show that when southern Chinese settle in other countries, their incidence of NPC is 10–30 times higher than that of other races, a rare pattern among malignancies suggesting a strong genetic component of NPC risk (9). A higher incidence of NPC is also observed among North African immigrants in Israel and Sweden, when compared to the native Israelis and native Swedes (10). Incidence of NPC among Chinese born in Western countries is still higher than that among Caucasians, although it is about half that of those living in China or migrating within Southeast Asia (10). In addition, compared with those born in southern France, men of French origin born in North Africa also had a higher incidence of NPC (11). The latter findings indicate that in addition to genetics, environmental factors also play an important role in NPC.

...

To date, established risk factors for type III NPC include Cantonese ethnicity (12), male sex (13), EBV infection, a family history of NPC, high consumption of salt-preserved fish, low intake of fresh vegetables and fruits intake, smoking, and some human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I alleles (14–17). On the other hand, other HLA genotypes and a history of infectious mononucleosis (IM) may be associated with a decreased risk (18). Further potential risk factors include high consumption of other preserved foods (19), a history of chronic respiratory tract conditions, and genetic polymorphisms in cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1), CYP2A6, glutathione S-transferase M1 (GSTM1) and GSTT1 (20,21). Less established risk factors include consumption of herbal medicine, occupational exposures to dust and formaldehyde, and nickel exposure (22).

...

## 7. Familial aggregation

...

Familial clustering has been consistently reported in NPC high-incidence (49), intermediate-incidence (50), and low-incidence (51) areas. In Southern China, where NPC is endemic, >5% of incident cases reported a positive family history of NPC among the first-degree relatives (52,53). Previous case-control studies in different populations showed that ORs ranged from 2 to 20 in individuals who reported a first-degree family history of NPC compared with those with no such history (54,55). This magnitude of association is among the highest of any malignancy, suggesting that environmental factors themselves cannot fully explain the observed association. Genes and environmental exposures likely play a combined role in the etiology of NPC. An inheritance pattern that cannot be explained by activation of a single major susceptibility gene is supported by results from a complex segregation analysis of familial NPC showing that the etiology of NPC involves interaction of multiple genetic and environmental factors (56).

...

Whether familial NPC cases differ substantially from sporadic cases in terms of clinical features (i.e. histology, stage and prognosis), ethnicity, sex, age at diagnosis, environment risk factors, EBV serology, and/or genetic risk factors is still controversial (57). A study in the recent past showed that familial cases did not have characteristics notably distinct from sporadic cases (58). On the other hand, others found that familial NPC cases tend to be younger, and have better survival than sporadic cases (59,60). Further, significant modification is reported of the association with family history of NPC by smoking, wood fuel use, and salt-preserved fish consumption, whereas a prospective study did not find an interaction between smoking and family history of NPC. The small number of controls with a positive first-degree family history of NPC and the low power of the statistical test of heterogeneity make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the joint effects of family history and environmental risk factors. Pooled studies with larger numbers of subjects will enable more powerful tests of such interactions.

...

To date, previous epidemiologic studies of NPC have been limited in number, size, scope and rigorousness of study design. Few studies have investigated the relative-specific risk among families with affected members. Because most studies have not ascertained all first-degree relatives and are not population-based, absolute NPC risks in the general population with and without a family history in NPC-endemic geographic regions, where the great majority of NPC cases occur worldwide, are largely unknown. The lack of evidence precludes cost-effectiveness modeling of screening for NPC among families with a positive history of NPC.

message.content:
**Short answer:** Nasopharyngeal cancer is rare in most of the world. The people at highest risk are those with ancestry from, or who live in, certain regions, especially southern China and Southeast Asia. Risk is also higher for people with a close relative who had it and for people with certain lifestyle exposures. Having a risk factor does not mean you will get the cancer, and most people with these factors never do.

**Where you live or where your ancestors come from**
- Fewer than 1 in 100,000 people worldwide are diagnosed each year. Most cases are in southern China, Southeast Asia, the Arctic, and the Middle East/North Africa. [NCI PDQ, health professional version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/hp/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq)
- The Canadian Cancer Society calls Southeast Asian or Chinese ancestry, particularly Cantonese ancestry, the most important risk factor. In North America, rates are highest among the Inuit. [Canadian Cancer Society](https://cancer.ca/en/cancer-information/cancer-types/nasopharyngeal/risks)
- Moving away doesn't remove the risk. People born in southern China who move to lower-risk countries have a lower risk than before, but it stays higher than for people native to those countries. The risk seems to fall over time and in later generations. [American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/nasopharyngeal-cancer/causes-risks-prevention.html)
- White people born in the US have a low risk, but White people born in China have a higher one. [American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/nasopharyngeal-cancer/causes-risks-prevention.html)

**Family history**
- Having a family member with nasopharyngeal cancer raises risk. [NCI patient version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq)
- A research review reported that a parent, brother, or sister with the cancer was linked to roughly a 4- to 20-fold higher risk. [AACR review](https://aacrjournals.org/cebp/article/30/6/1035/670828/The-Evolving-Epidemiology-of-Nasopharyngeal)
- The American Cancer Society says it isn't known whether this comes from shared genes, shared environment such as diet, or both. [American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/nasopharyngeal-cancer/causes-risks-prevention.html)

**Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)**
- EBV infection is a listed risk factor. [NCI patient version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq)
- One review says EBV appears to be a necessary cause of the common undifferentiated type but is not enough on its own. Other factors, such as genes and environment, likely play a role too. [Review, PMC5844099](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5844099/)
- EBV infection is very common, so it doesn't by itself put someone at high risk. That point is my own, not a claim from the sources.

**Diet and habits**
- Eating a lot of salt-cured fish and meats is linked to higher risk. This includes Chinese-style salted fish, especially when it was fed to children at weaning. [Canadian Cancer Society](https://cancer.ca/en/cancer-information/cancer-types/nasopharyngeal/risks)
- One newer study found a smaller role for salted fish than older studies did. [AACR review](https://aacrjournals.org/cebp/article/30/6/1035/670828/The-Evolving-Epidemiology-of-Nasopharyngeal)
- Tobacco use, secondhand smoke, and frequent heavy alcohol use are listed risk factors. [NCI patient version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq)
- In a southern China study, current male smokers had higher risk, but men who had quit at least 4 years earlier did not. [AACR review](https://aacrjournals.org/cebp/article/30/6/1035/670828/The-Evolving-Epidemiology-of-Nasopharyngeal)

**Sex and age**
- It is more common in men. In most populations, rates in men are two to three times those in women. [AACR review](https://aacrjournals.org/cebp/article/30/6/1035/670828/The-Evolving-Epidemiology-of-Nasopharyngeal)
- Where the cancer is uncommon, it is more often diagnosed after age 50. In high-risk areas, younger people are more often affected. [NCI patient version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/head-and-neck/patient/adult/nasopharyngeal-treatment-pdq)

**Other possible links**
- HIV/AIDS was associated with about double the incidence in one review. [AACR review](https://aacrjournals.org/cebp/article/30/6/1035/670828/The-Evolving-Epidemiology-of-Nasopharyngeal)
- Low socioeconomic status is also linked to higher risk. [Canadian Cancer Society](https://cancer.ca/en/cancer-information/cancer-types/nasopharyngeal/risks)

**What to do:** If you fall into a higher-risk group, tell your doctor about your family history. Also report symptoms that don't go away, such as a lump in the neck, blocked nose on one side, nosebleeds, or ear problems. I didn't find a source in these results listing symptoms, so that advice is general rather than sourced. I also didn't find a recommendation for routine screening in the general population. The sources mention EBV blood tests only for early detection in a few high-incidence areas. [Review, PMC5844099](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5844099/)

**You catch ringworm through contact with the fungi that cause it—not from a worm.** It is a contagious infection that can affect the skin, scalp, or nails. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/about/index.html)

It can spread through:
- **Skin-to-skin contact with an infected person**, including during contact sports or intimate/sexual contact. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html)
- **Touching an infected animal**, such as petting or grooming a dog or cat with ringworm. [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/ringworm-body/symptoms-causes/syc-20353780)
- **Sharing contaminated items**, such as towels, clothing, bedding, combs, or brushes. [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/ringworm-body/symptoms-causes/syc-20353780)
- **Contact with contaminated surfaces**, such as walking barefoot on locker-room or public-shower floors. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)
- **Rarely, contact with infected soil.** Mayo Clinic says this would most likely require prolonged contact with heavily infected soil. [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/ringworm-body/symptoms-causes/syc-20353780)

**To reduce your risk:** keep skin clean and dry, don’t share towels or other personal items, wear protective footwear in communal showers, wash your hands after touching pets, and avoid skin-to-skin contact with someone who has known or suspected ringworm. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/about/index.html)

If you develop an itchy, scaly rash, have it checked—other skin conditions can look like ringworm, and testing can help identify the right treatment. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/about/index.html)

message.content:
**You catch ringworm by coming into contact with the fungus that causes it.** It isn't caused by a worm. The CDC says it's a fungal infection that spreads easily ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html)).

**Main ways it spreads**
- **Skin-to-skin contact with an infected person.** The CDC includes sexual contact in this ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html)).
- **Contact with an infected animal.** Pets can pass it to people. The CDC mentions pets generally, and NI Direct names dogs and cats and says you can catch it by stroking them ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html); [NI Direct](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/conditions/ringworm)).
- **Shared objects.** Examples are towels, bedsheets and combs ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html); [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ringworm/)). The WHO also lists clothing and sports equipment ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ringworm-(tinea))).
- **Contaminated surfaces.** The CDC gives locker room floors as an example ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html)). The CDC's clinical page for health professionals also lists shower stall floors ([CDC clinical overview](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)). The WHO says fungi thrive in warm, moist places such as showers, locker rooms and swimming pools ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ringworm-(tinea))).
- **Soil.** The NHS says infected soil can spread it, though this is less common ([NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ringworm/)). The WHO also lists contact with fungi in soil ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ringworm-(tinea))).

**Other points**
- **Timing:** The CDC's clinical page says symptoms usually start 4–14 days after exposure ([CDC clinical overview](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)).
- **Spread on your own body:** It can spread from one body part to another ([CDC clinical overview](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)). The NHS advises not scratching the rash because that could spread it ([NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ringworm/)).
- **Nails:** Nail ringworm usually spreads through a small cut in the skin around the nail. Foot and between-the-toes infections often go along with it ([CDC clinical overview](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)).

**Who is more at risk**
- **Athletes:** Contact sports such as wrestling, heavy sweating, shared equipment and bare feet in locker rooms raise the risk ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html); [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ringworm-(tinea))).
- **People with weakened immune systems:** The CDC says they may be especially at risk, and the WHO says they are more susceptible ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/about/index.html); [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ringworm-(tinea))).
- **Certain habits:** The CDC lists going several days without washing, not changing socks and underwear daily, and walking barefoot in shared spaces like dressing rooms ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/causes/index.html)).

**How to lower your risk**
- Keep your skin clean and dry.
- Wear sandals or shoes in public showers and locker rooms.
- Don't share towels, socks, sports gear or combs.
- Wash your hands after touching pets.
- Have a pet checked by a vet if it has patches of missing fur.

These tips come from the [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/about/index.html), [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ringworm-(tinea)) and [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ringworm/).

**Caveat:** Ringworm can look like other rashes. The CDC recommends testing to confirm it before treatment ([CDC clinical overview](https://www.cdc.gov/ringworm/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html)). See a healthcare provider if you aren't sure what you have.

Question: What do the cancerous moles look like?

message.content:
**A cancerous mole—usually referring to melanoma—may look uneven, have several colors, or change over time. But melanoma can also appear as a new spot rather than an existing mole, and appearance alone cannot confirm cancer.** Diagnosis requires a biopsy, where tissue is examined under a microscope. [National Cancer Institute (NCI)](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/moles-fact-sheet)

### Look for the “ABCDE” warning signs
- **A — Asymmetry:** One half does not match the other.
- **B — Border:** The edges are irregular, jagged, scalloped, or blurry.
- **C — Color:** Uneven color or a mixture of tan, brown, black, white, red, or blue.
- **D — Diameter:** Often larger than **6 mm**, about the width of a pencil eraser—but melanoma **can be smaller**.
- **E — Evolving:** The spot changes in size, shape, or color, or looks different from your other spots. [American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/abcdes-melanoma)

**Not all melanomas are dark or flat.** Some are pink or red, look like a sore, or form a firm, raised, dome-shaped growth. Melanoma under a nail may look like a dark vertical line. [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/types/common/melanoma/symptoms)

An ordinary mole is typically round or oval, evenly colored, and stable. However, some noncancerous “atypical” moles also have irregular borders or mixed colors, so an unusual appearance does **not automatically mean cancer**. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/moles-fact-sheet)

### What to do
**Arrange a prompt appointment with a dermatologist** if a spot is new and unusual, looks different from your others, changes, itches, or bleeds. A sore that does not heal also needs checking. You do not need to wait for every ABCDE sign to appear. [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/types/common/melanoma/symptoms)

For **photographs of melanoma and its different appearances**, see the [AAD’s illustrated guide](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/types/common/melanoma/symptoms).

url_citation.content:
## What's the difference between a mole and melanoma?

...

People often want to know how they can tell a mole from a melanoma. Here is a general rule.

...

### Mole

...

A mole on your body usually has these traits. It's:

...

- One color—often brown, but a mole can be tan, black, red, pink, blue, skin-toned, or colorless
- Round in shape
- Flat or slightly raised
- Unchanged from month to month

...

Although moles have a distinct look, they may not look alike. Even in the same person, moles can differ in size, shape, or color. Moles can have hair. Some moles will change slowly over time, possibly even disappearing.

...

It's also important to know that moles can appear anywhere on the skin. They can develop on your scalp, between your fingers and toes, on the soles and palms, and even under your nails.

...

### Melanoma

...

The most-serious skin cancer differs from moles in that it tends to show one or more of the following traits:

...

A = Asymmetry. One half is unlike the other.

...

B = Border. An irregular, scalloped, or poorly defined border.

...

C = Color. Is varied from one area to another; has shades of tan, brown, or black; is sometimes white, red, or blue.

...

D = Diameter. Melanoma are usually greater than 6 mm (the size of a pencil eraser) when diagnosed, but they can be smaller.

...

E = Evolving. A mole or skin lesion that looks different from the rest or is changing in size, shape, or color.​

...

If you see a mole or new spot on your skin that has any of the ABCDEs of melanoma, immediately make an appointment to see a dermatologist.

url_citation.title: Common Moles, Dysplastic Nevi, and Risk of Melanoma
url_citation.content:
What does a common mole look like?

...

A common mole is usually smaller than about 5 millimeters wide (about 1/4 inch, the width of a pencil eraser). It is round or oval, has a smooth surface with a distinct edge, and is often dome-shaped. A common mole usually has an even color of pink, tan, or brown. People who have dark skin or hair tend to have darker moles than people with fair skin or blonde hair. Several photos of common moles are shown here, and What Does a Mole Look Like? has more examples.

...

Can a common mole turn into melanoma?

...

Only rarely does a common mole turn into melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer.

...

Although common moles are not cancerous, people who have many small moles or several large ones have an increased risk of developing melanoma (1).

...

Certain changes in a mole may indicate that it is turning into a melanoma (2). People should tell their doctor if they notice

...

- The color of the mole changes
- The mole gets unevenly smaller or bigger (unlike normal moles in children, which get evenly bigger)
- The mole changes in shape, texture, or height
- The skin on the surface of the mole becomes dry or scaly
- The mole becomes hard or feels lumpy
- The mole starts to itch
- The mole bleeds or oozes

...

What is a dysplastic nevus?

...

A dysplastic nevus is a type of mole that looks different from a common mole. (Some doctors use the term "atypical mole" to refer to a dysplastic nevus.) A dysplastic nevus may be bigger than a common mole, and its color, surface, and border may be different. It is usually more than 5 millimeters wide (1, 3). A dysplastic nevus can have a mixture of several colors, from pink to dark brown. It is usually flat, with a smooth, slightly scaly, or pebbly surface, and it has an irregular edge that may fade into the surrounding skin. Some examples of dysplastic nevi are shown here. What Does a Mole Look Like? has more examples.

...

This dysplastic nevus has a raised area at the center that doctors may call a “fried egg” appearance.

...

Can a dysplastic nevus turn into melanoma?

...

Only rarely does a dysplastic nevus turn into melanoma (1, 3). However, dysplastic nevi are a risk factor for developing melanoma, and the more dysplastic nevi a person has, the greater their risk of developing melanoma (1, 3). Researchers estimate that the risk of melanoma is about 10 times greater for someone with more than five dysplastic nevi than for someone who has none.

...

Should people have a doctor remove a dysplastic nevus or a common mole to prevent it from changing into melanoma?

...

No. Normally, people do not need to have a dysplastic nevus or a common mole removed. One reason is that very few dysplastic nevi or common moles turn into melanoma (1, 3). And most melanomas do not start as common moles or dysplastic nevi (2). That is why doctors usually remove only moles that have changed or new colored or otherwise suspicious areas on the skin.

...

What does melanoma look like?

...

Often the first sign of melanoma is a change in the shape, color, size, or feel of an existing mole. Melanoma may also appear as a new colored or otherwise unusual area on the skin.

...

The "ABCDE" rule describes the features of early melanoma (2, 6):

...

- Asymmetry. The shape of one half does not match the other half.
- Border that is irregular. The edges are often ragged, notched, or blurred in outline. The pigment may spread into the surrounding skin.
- Color that is uneven. Shades of black, brown, and tan may be present. Areas of white, gray, red, pink, or blue may also be seen.
- Diameter. There is a change in size, usually an increase. Melanomas can be tiny, but most are larger than 6 millimeters wide (about 1/4 inch wide).
- Evolving. The mole has changed over the past few weeks or months.

...

Melanomas can vary greatly in how they look. Many melanomas show all of the ABCDE features. However, some may show only one or two of the ABCDE features (6). Several photos of melanomas are shown here. More photos are on the What Does Melanoma Look Like? page.

...

An uneven (asymmetric) melanoma with an irregular but distinct border. The melanoma is more than 20 millimeters wide (about the size of a postage stamp).

...

A blue-black melanoma that has irregular and scalloped borders. It has arisen from a dysplastic nevus (the pink-tan region at the upper left). The melanoma is about 12 millimeters wide (nearly 1/2 inch).

...

In advanced melanoma, the texture of the mole may change. The skin on the surface may break down and look scraped. The mole may become hard or lumpy and the surface may ooze or bleed. Sometimes the melanoma is itchy, tender, or painful.

...

How is melanoma diagnosed?

...

The only way to diagnose melanoma is to remove tissue and check it for cancer cells. The doctor will remove all or part of the skin that looks abnormal. Usually, this procedure takes only a few minutes and can be done in a doctor's office, clinic, or hospital. The sample will be sent to a lab and a pathologist will look at the tissue under a microscope to check for melanoma.

...

What are the differences between a common mole, a dysplastic nevus, and a melanoma?

...

Common moles, dysplastic nevi, and melanoma vary by size, color, shape, and surface texture. The table below summarizes some differences between moles and cancer. Another important difference is that a common mole or dysplastic nevus will not return after it is removed by a full excisional biopsy from the skin, but melanoma sometimes grows back. Also, melanoma is cancer, so it can spread to other parts of the body.

Question: What do the cancerous moles look like?

message.content:
**Short answer:** A cancerous mole, which is usually melanoma, often looks uneven or changing. It may be asymmetrical, have a ragged border, have several colors, be larger than a pea, or be changing. Some melanomas don't look like that, so you can't rule cancer out by sight. Only a doctor's test of a skin sample can diagnose it.

**The ABCDE checklist**
- **Asymmetry:** one half doesn't match the other half. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/melanoma-photos)
- **Border:** the edges are ragged, notched, scalloped, or blurred. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/melanoma-photos), [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/abcdes-melanoma)
- **Color:** the color is uneven. It may include tan, brown, or black, and sometimes white, gray, red, pink, or blue. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/melanoma-photos), [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/abcdes-melanoma)
- **Diameter:** most melanomas are larger than about 6 mm (a pencil eraser or small pea). They can be smaller. [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/abcdes-melanoma)
- **Evolving:** the mole changes in size, shape, or color over weeks or months. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/melanoma-photos)

**Other warning signs**
- **A new spot:** melanoma can appear as a new mole rather than a change in an old one. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/melanoma-photos)
- **The "ugly duckling":** a spot that looks different from your other moles. [DermNet](https://dermnetnz.org/topics/check-your-skin-today) In one small experiment, nine dermatologists labeled every melanoma among 80 patients' moles as an "ugly duckling." [JAMA Dermatology](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamadermatology/fullarticle/2600689)
- **Itching, pain, or bleeding:** a spot may itch, hurt, or bleed. Some melanomas cause no discomfort. [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/types/common/melanoma/symptoms)
- **Advanced melanoma:** the surface may break down, look scraped, become hard or lumpy, or ooze or bleed. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/melanoma-photos)
- **Nails:** a dark brown or black vertical line under a fingernail or toenail can be a sign. [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/types/common/melanoma/symptoms)

**Melanomas that don't follow the rules**
- Many show all the ABCDE features, but some show only one or two. [NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/types/skin/melanoma-photos)
- Nodular melanoma tends to skip the early flat stage. DermNet describes it as raised, firm, and growing quickly over days to weeks (the "EFG" signs). [DermNet](https://dermnetnz.org/topics/check-your-skin-today)
- Australian guidelines say dangerous melanomas can be symmetrical, dome-shaped, and skin-colored. They advise that any lesion that is raised, firm, and growing for more than a month should raise suspicion. [Cancer Council Australia guidelines](https://cdn.craft.cloud/019efd17-dcc2-707f-8e07-011d00d1146a/assets/issues/10.5694mja17.00123.pdf)
- Melanoma can look different on Black and brown skin than on white skin. [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/melanoma/in-depth/melanoma/art-20546856)

**What to do**
- See a doctor, ideally a dermatologist, if a spot has any of these features, is changing, or is itching or bleeding. [AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/abcdes-melanoma)
- Don't wait for several warning signs to appear.
- Photos help a lot. The AAD, NCI, and Mayo Clinic pages linked above have example pictures.

The sources above focus on melanoma. Other skin cancers, such as basal and squamous cell carcinoma, can look different. The CDC lists a sore that doesn't heal as one sign. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/skin-cancer/symptoms/index.html)

Abstract Introduction: A Cancer Council Australia multidisciplinary working group is currently revising and updating the 2008 evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for the management of cutaneous melanoma. While there have been many recent improvements in treatment options for metastatic melanoma, early diagnosis remains critical to reducing mortality from the disease. Improved awareness of the atypical presentations of this common malignancy is required to achieve this. A chapter of the new guidelines was therefore developed to aid recognition of atypical melanomas. Main recommendations: Because thick, life-threatening melanomas may lack the more classical ABCD (asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variegation, diameter > 6 mm) features of melanoma, a thorough history of the lesion with regard to change in morphology and growth over time is essential. Any lesion that is changing in morphology or growing over a period of more than one month should be excised or referred for prompt expert opinion. Changes in management as a result of the guidelines: These guidelines provide greater emphasis on improved recognition of the atypical presentations of melanoma, in particular nodular, desmoplastic and acral lentiginous subtypes, with particular awareness of hypomelanotic and amelanotic lesions.

If these changes have been accurately recognised by the patient or if there is photographic evidence to demonstrate stability or change, this may be very helpful in determining the index of suspicion. Radial growth phase melanomas change in size, shape or colour, and vertical growth phase melanomas evolve with elevation and ulceration and may bleed. A history of the duration of a lesion and any change in its appearance is a minimum requirement for the assessment of any potential skin cancer.

question: What is causing shivering?
prompt:
Search the web before answering this consumer health question. Answer in English for a lay reader. Give a direct, useful answer, cite the sources immediately after the statements they support, and preserve source-specific uncertainty and scope. Do not claim a source supports a statement unless it does.

Question: What is causing shivering?

message.content:
**Shivering usually means your body is trying to make heat**, either because you are cold or because a fever is developing. Your muscles rapidly tighten and relax to generate warmth; chills can start before a fever becomes obvious. [MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003091.htm) Shivering alone is not enough to tell what is causing it in your case.

### Possible causes
- **Cold exposure:** Cold air, wet clothing or cold water can trigger shivering. More severe cooling can cause hypothermia—a dangerous body temperature below **35°C (95°F)**. [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hypothermia/)
- **An infection:** Flu and other viral infections, pneumonia and urinary tract infections can cause chills, often with fever. You can also have chills without a fever. [Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills)
- **Other triggers:** Panic attacks, low blood sugar in people with diabetes, drug withdrawal, menopausal hot flashes and recovery from general anesthesia can also cause shivering or shaking. [Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills)

### What to do now
**Check your temperature**, if possible. Feeling shivery can accompany a fever even when the thermometer reads below 38°C (100.4°F). [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/fever-in-adults/)

- If you have been cold or wet, move somewhere sheltered, remove wet clothing and use dry clothes or a blanket. If fully awake, a warm non-alcoholic drink can help. [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hypothermia/)
- If you have a fever, rest and drink fluids; avoid piling on heavy blankets or using ice-cold baths, which can worsen chills. [MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003091.htm)
- Seek medical advice promptly if chills accompany a bad cough, abdominal pain, burning or frequent urination, or a fever that is not improving. [MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003091.htm)

### When it is urgent
**Call your local emergency number** if shivering comes with confusion, slurred speech, difficulty breathing, blue/grey or blotchy skin, or you feel seriously unwell—these can be signs of sepsis. Shivering by itself does **not** establish that diagnosis. [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/)

Also get emergency help for suspected hypothermia, especially after cold exposure with confusion, slow breathing or a temperature below 35°C (95°F). [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hypothermia/)

**How old is the person, how long has the shivering lasted, what is their temperature, and are there other symptoms or recent cold exposure?**

url_citation.title: Sepsis - NHS
url_citation.content:
Sepsis is a serious reaction to an infection that can be life-threatening. It develops very quickly and needs urgent treatment in hospital.

...

## Symptoms of sepsis

...

Sepsis usually develops quickly over a few hours. If it's not treated it can turn into septic shock, which you can die from.

...

### Symptoms of sepsis in adults

...

Common symptoms of sepsis in adults include:

...

- confusion or slurred speech
- uncontrollable shivering
- muscle pain
- difficulty breathing
- blue, pale, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue – on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands or soles of the feet
- a high or low temperature – a high temperature is less common in older adults
- not peeing all day or peeing very little in the past 18 hours

...

A child or adult with sepsis might not have every symptom listed. Get immediate medical help if you or your child are unwell and you think there's something seriously wrong.

...

You need to get medical help immediately if you think you or your child might have sepsis.

...

#### A baby or child under 5 years:

...

- is breathing very fast or having difficulty breathing – they may make grunting noises or their tummy may be sucking under their ribcage when they breathe
- has blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue – on black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands or soles of the feet
- has a rash that does not fade when you press it
- has a very high temperature – 38C or more in babies under 3 months old, or 39C or more in babies 3 to 6 months old
- has a very low temperature – less than 36C, or feels cold to the touch or is shivery
- has a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry
- is not responding like they normally do, is not feeding, is difficult to wake or is more sleepy than usual
- has not had a pee for the last 12 hours
- has symptoms you're worried might be sepsis

...

#### An adult or child aged 5 years or over:

...

- is breathing very fast
- is confused, has slurred speech, or is not making sense
- has blue, pale or blotchy skin – on black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands or soles of the feet
- has a very high or very low temperature, feels hot or cold to the touch, or is shivery
- has a rash that does not fade when you press it
- has symptoms you're worried might be sepsis

...

### Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:

...

- you or your child have had sepsis in the past 12 months and have symptoms of an infection, such as a very high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery

...

## Causes of sepsis

...

The exact cause of sepsis is not known. It's thought your immune system overreacts to an infection and starts to damage your body's organs.

...

The risk of getting sepsis may also be affected by the type of infection, your age, genetics and any other conditions you have.

...

Any type of infection can lead to sepsis, but bacterial infections are the most common cause, including:

...

- chest infections (pneumonia)
- urinary tract infections (UTIs)
- abdominal infections, such as appendicitis
- skin infections, such as cellulitis or infected wounds

...

Anyone can get sepsis, but there's a higher chance of getting it if:

...

- a baby is under 12 months
- you're over 75 years
- you're pregnant, have given birth, or had an abortion or a miscarriage in the past 6 weeks
- your immune system is weakened because you have a condition like HIV or sickle cell disease, you're having chemotherapy, or you're taking corticosteroids or immunosuppressants
- you have a burn, cut or wound, or a skin infection like cellulitis
- you have a catheter (a tube used to empty pee from your bladder and collect it in a drainage bag)
- you inject illegal drugs or misuse alcohol

Normal body temperature is different for everyone and changes during the day.

# Hypothermia

...

Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35C (normal body temperature is around 37C). It's a medical emergency that needs to be treated in hospital.

...

## Symptoms of hypothermia

...

Symptoms of hypothermia include:

...

- shivering
- pale, cold and dry skin – skin and lips may turn blue or grey (on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet)
- slurred speech
- slow breathing
- tiredness or confusion

...

## Immediate action required: Go to A&E or call 999 if:

...

- you think you or your child have hypothermia

...

- move the person indoors or somewhere sheltered as quickly as possible
- remove any wet clothing, wrap them in a blanket, sleeping bag or dry towel, making sure their head is covered
- give them a warm non-alcoholic drink and some sugary food like chocolate if they're fully awake
- keep them awake by talking to them until help arrives
- make sure you or someone else stays with them

...

## Treatment in hospital for hypothermia

...

If you have hypothermia, you’ll usually be treated in hospital.

...

Your heart rate will be monitored and you may be given oxygen to help you breathe.

...

You may also be given warm fluids straight into a vein to help your body warm up.

...

Treatment in intensive care may be needed if you have severe hypothermia.

...

## Causes of hypothermia

...

Hypothermia happens when you get too cold and your body temperature drops below 35C.

You can get hypothermia if you:

...

- do not wear enough clothes in cold weather
- stay out in the cold too long
- fall into cold water
- have wet clothes and get cold
- live in a cold house – older people living alone are particularly at risk

Chills (shivering) may occur at the start of an infection. They are most often associated with a fever. Chills are caused by rapid muscle contraction and relaxation. ...

Fever (which can accompany chills) is the body's natural response to a variety of conditions, such as infections. If the fever is mild, 102°F (38.8°C) or less, with no side effects, you do not need to see a provider for treatment. You can treat the problem at home by drinking lots of fluids and getting plenty of rest.

...

Evaporation cools the skin and reduces body temperature. Sponging with lukewarm water, about 70°F (21.1°C), may help reduce a fever. Cold water may increase the fever as it can trigger chills.

...

Medicines such as acetaminophen, aspirin, or ibuprofen are helpful in fighting a fever and chills.

...

HOME CARE FOR A CHILD

...

If the child's temperature is causing the child to be uncomfortable, give pain-relieving tablets or liquid. Non-aspirin pain-relievers such as acetaminophen are recommended. Ibuprofen may also be used. Follow the dosage guidelines on the package label.

...

Note: DO NOT give aspirin to treat fever in a child younger than 19 years old because of the risk for Reye syndrome.

Other things to help the child feel more comfortable include:

url_citation.title: Chills: Causes & Treatment
url_citation.content:
Chills are your body’s way of raising its core temperature. Cold temperatures, viruses, infections and other illnesses can bring on chills. When you shiver, your muscles relax and contract. This involuntary movement warms your body. Chills and fever often go together. But not everyone with a fever gets chills. And you can get chills with no fever.

...

These are involuntary body responses. Involuntary means you can’t consciously control them. Shivering causes your muscles to contract and relax, which warms up your body.

...

Sometimes you might get cold chills from being exposed to low temperatures. Shivering can also be a sign that your body is fighting off an illness, infection or another health problem.

...

### What causes chills?

...

You experience chills when your body’s core temperature drops. For most people, the average core temperature hovers around 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit (37 degrees Celsius). A “normal” temperature can vary between 97 F and 99 F, though.

...

Your body’s temperature naturally varies. But very low temperatures are dangerous. Exposure to extreme cold can lead to hypothermia (low body temperature). This problem occurs when body temperature drops below 95 F (35 C).

...

These health conditions can also make you shiver:

...

- Bacterial infections like listeria, pneumonia and urinary tract infections (UTIs).
- Cancers, such as leukemia.
- Drug withdrawal (substance abuse).
- Hangover.
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) in people with diabetes.
- Menopausal night sweats or hot flashes.
- Panic attacks.
- Parasite infections like giardiasis.
- Sepsis.
- Viruses, including those that cause the flu.

...

As many as two in three people experience chills and shivering after receiving general anesthesia for a surgery. Even if you aren’t feeling cold, a drop in body temperature may cause you to shiver as you come out of the anesthesia.

...

Some people tremble from a surge of adrenaline after a traumatic event like an accident or near accident. Psychological trauma, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), may also make you feel shaky.

...

### How are chills treated?

...

Layering clothes or getting to a warm place can make cold chills go away. You can also drink hot chocolate, coffee or tea to raise your internal body temperature.

...

If an illness, infection or another health problem causes chills, treating the condition should get rid of the symptom. Treatments vary depending on the underlying cause. They may include:

...

- Antibiotics for bacterial and parasitic infections.
- Antiviral medications for viral infections.
- Over-the-counter medicine, such as acetaminophen (Tylenol®) or ibuprofen (Advil®), for conditions like flu that cause fevers and chills.

...

## When To Call the Doctor

...

### When should I contact a healthcare provider?

...

You should contact your healthcare provider if you experience body chills and:

...

- Temperature above 104 F (40 C) or below 95 F (35 C) in an adult or a child older than three.
- Temperature above 102.2 F (39 C) in a child aged three months to three years.
- Temperature above 100.4 F (38 C) in an infant younger than three months.
- Chest pain or unexplained pain.
- Extreme fatigue.
- Severe abdominal pain.
- Wheezing or difficulty breathing.

...

### What questions should I ask my healthcare provider?

...

You may want to ask your healthcare provider:

...

- What is causing my chills?
- How should I treat chills?
- Should I look out for signs of complications?

...

Chills can cause an uncomfortable sensation of shivering and goosebumps. They’re often a sign that your body feels too cold or is fighting off an illness. Many people feel chilled when they have a fever. Warming your body with more clothes and heat can ward off cold chills. If a sickness causes chills, see your healthcare provider. Most chills pass within a few hours or days. In the meantime, pile on the blankets and make a cup of tea.

message.content:
**Shivering is your body trying to make heat.** Muscles rapidly tense and relax without your control, and that produces warmth. The cause is usually one of the following.

**Common causes**
- **Cold.** Shivering is an automatic defense against cold, and it starts when your body temperature begins to drop ([Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/hypothermia/symptoms-causes/syc-20352682)). Wind or wet clothing can make it worse ([Healthline](https://www.healthline.com/health/shivering)).
- **Fever or infection.** Chills often come at the start of an infection and usually go with a fever. They can come before the fever rises ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003091.htm)).
  - During a fever, your brain's "thermostat" in the hypothalamus is reset higher. Your body may shiver to reach that new target ([Merck Manual](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/infectious-diseases/biology-of-infectious-disease/fever)).
  - Not everyone with a fever gets chills, and you can get chills without a fever ([Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills)).
- **Other health conditions.** Cleveland Clinic lists these as possible causes:
  - Infections such as pneumonia or UTIs
  - Sepsis
  - Low blood sugar in people with diabetes
  - Drug withdrawal
  - Hangover
  - Menopausal hot flashes
  - Panic attacks
  - Some cancers, such as leukemia

  ([Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills)). Healthline also says low blood sugar can trigger shivering, including in people who haven't eaten for a while ([Healthline](https://www.healthline.com/health/shivering)).
- **Adrenaline.** Fear, or a shock such as a near-accident, can cause shivering or trembling ([Healthline](https://www.healthline.com/health/shivering); [Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills)).
- **After surgery.** As many as two in three people have chills or shivering after general anesthesia, even if they don't feel cold ([Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills)).
- **Feeling cold more easily.** An underactive thyroid can make you feel cold more acutely. If you're getting cold more often than you used to, Healthline suggests telling your doctor, since your thyroid may need checking ([Healthline](https://www.healthline.com/health/shivering)).

**What to do**
- If you're just cold and warming up (a sweater, a warmer room) fixes it, you probably don't need a doctor ([Healthline](https://www.healthline.com/health/shivering)).
- For a mild fever of 102°F (38.8°C) or lower with no other problems, MedlinePlus says you can usually treat it at home with fluids and rest ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003091.htm)).

**When to get medical help**
- **Suspected hypothermia.** This means a body temperature below 95°F (35°C). Mayo Clinic calls it a medical emergency and says to call 911 ([Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/hypothermia/symptoms-causes/syc-20352682)).
  - Warning signs include confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness, clumsiness, a weak pulse and slow, shallow breathing ([Mayo Clinic first aid](https://www.mayoclinic.org/first-aid/first-aid-hypothermia/basics/art-20056624)).
  - Shivering may stop as body temperature falls further, so no shivering doesn't mean someone is safe ([Mayo Clinic first aid](https://www.mayoclinic.org/first-aid/first-aid-hypothermia/basics/art-20056624)).
- **Chills with other warning signs.** Cleveland Clinic says to contact a provider if chills come with any of these ([Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/21476-chills)):
  - A temperature above 104°F (40°C) in an adult
  - A temperature above 102.2°F (39°C) in a child aged 3 months to 3 years
  - A temperature above 100.4°F (38°C) in an infant under 3 months
  - Chest pain
  - Severe abdominal pain
  - Trouble breathing
  - Extreme fatigue
- **Urgent symptoms with a fever or chills.** Medical News Today lists a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade under a pressed glass, confusion, seizures, a blue tinge to the lips or nails, and fast or shallow breathing ([Medical News Today](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/chills)).
- **Persistent chills.** See a doctor if they don't improve, don't respond to fever reducers, or keep coming back ([Medical News Today](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/chills)).
- **Possible malaria.** Chills are a classic symptom. If you've lived in or recently visited an area where malaria occurs, speak to a doctor right away ([Medical News Today](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/324864)).

These sources are general health information and can't tell you the cause in your case. If you tell me more, I can help narrow it down. Useful details are whether you have a fever, how long it has lasted, any recent illness, surgery or medications, and whether you feel cold.

url_citation.title: Physiology, Temperature Regulation
url_citation.content:
The human body's thermostat is the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center, which, more specifically, is located in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus. This center sets the body's set point and regulates temperature homeostasis. The hypothalamus contains temperature sensors, which receive information via nerve cells called thermoreceptors. The body has peripheral and central thermoreceptors. The peripheral thermoreceptors are located in the skin and sense surface temperatures, while central thermoreceptors are found in the viscera, spinal cord, and hypothalamus and sense the core temperature. Variations in body temperature activate these thermoreceptors, which inform the preoptic area of the hypothalamus. This area then activates heat regulation mechanisms to increase or decrease body temperature and return it to baseline.[2]

...

The definition of 'fever' is an elevation in core body temperature above a set point, which is set by the preoptic area of the hypothalamus in the thermoregulatory center. Numerous causes can precipitate a fever, including infection, inflammation, autoimmune processes, medications, or malignancy. These processes involve the release of immunological mediators, which trigger the thermoregulatory center of the hypothalamus, leading to an increase in the body's core temperature.[4]

...

The febrile response is mediated by pyrogens, substances that induce fever. Exogenous pyrogens originate outside the body and induce interleukins. Endogenous pyrogens originate inside the body and act on the thermoregulatory center in the hypothalamus. The primary endogenous pyrogens (cytokines) include interleukin-1 (IL-1) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha).[5]

...

These pyrogens induce cyclooxygenase 2 (COX2), which catalyzes the formation of prostaglandins (PG) from arachidonic acid. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) then stimulates the release of neurotransmitters (cAMP), increasing body temperature. Interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) is another proinflammatory cytokine that can directly cause fever via induction of IL-1 and synthesis of TNF.[6]

...

The mechanism of thermoregulation involves afferent sensing, central control, and efferent responses. Peripheral and central thermoreceptors sense an increase or decrease in body temperature and send this information to the hypothalamus. The body then responds with multiple mechanisms to either dissipate or generate heat based on the body's needs. The physiological and behavioral responses to the activation of thermoreceptors are as follows.[11]

...

The body responds by generating heat via:

...

Activating the sympathetic nervous system which causes vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, causing blood to bypass the skin and leading to a decreased loss of heat. Additionally, adrenal glands will release catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine), leading to increased metabolic rate and heat production. Piloerection (goosebumps) also occur, leading to heat-trapping.

...

Releasing thyroid hormones from the hypothalamus causes an increased metabolic rate and subsequent heat production.

...

Activating the primary motor center in the posterior hypothalamus causes skeletal muscle contraction and shivering, leading to increased heat production.

url_citation.content:
Fever is an elevated body temperature that occurs when the body's thermostat (located in the hypothalamus) resets at a higher temperature, primarily in response to an infection. Elevated body temperature that is not caused by a resetting of the temperature set point is called hyperthermia.

...

Symptoms are due mainly to the condition causing the fever, although fever itself can cause chills, sweats, and discomfort and make patients feel flushed and warm.

...

Body temperature is determined by the balance between heat production by tissues, particularly the liver and muscles, and heat loss from the periphery. Normally, the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center maintains the internal temperature between 37° and 38° C. Fever results when something raises the hypothalamic set point, triggering vasoconstriction and shunting of blood from the periphery to decrease heat loss; sometimes shivering, which increases heat production, is induced. These processes continue until the temperature of the blood bathing the hypothalamus reaches the new set point. Resetting the hypothalamic set point downward (eg, with antipyretics) initiates heat loss through sweating and vasodilation.

...

Pyrogens are substances that cause fever. Exogenous pyrogens are usually microbes or their products. The best studied are the lipopolysaccharides of gram-negative bacteria (commonly called endotoxins) and Staphylococcus aureus toxin, which causes toxic shock syndrome. Fever is the result of exogenous pyrogens that induce release of endogenous pyrogens, such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), and IL-6 and other cytokines, which then trigger cytokine receptors, or of exogenous pyrogens that directly trigger Toll-like receptors in the different intestinal epithelial lineages.

...

Prostaglandin E2 synthesis appears to play a critical role.

...

Many disorders can cause fever. They are broadly categorized as

...

- Infectious (most common) 
- Neoplastic
- Inflammatory (including rheumatic, nonrheumatic, and drug-related)

...

The cause of an acute (ie, duration ≤ 4 days) fever in adults is highly likely to be infectious. When patients present with fever due to a noninfectious cause, the fever is almost always chronic or recurrent. Also, an isolated, acute febrile event in patients with a known inflammatory or neoplastic disorder is still most likely to be infectious. In healthy people, an acute febrile event is unlikely to be the initial manifestation of a chronic illness.

...

### Infectious causes

...

Virtually all infectious illnesses can cause fever. But overall, the most likely causes are 

- Upper and lower respiratory tract infections
- Gastrointestinal infections
- Urinary tract infections
- Skin infections

...

Most acute respiratory tract and gastrointestinal infections are viral.

...

Specific patient and external factors also influence which causes are most likely.

...

Patient factors include health status, age, occupation, and risk factors (eg, hospitalization, recent invasive procedures, presence of IV or urinary catheters, use of mechanical ventilation).

...

External factors are those that expose patients to specific diseases—eg, through infected contacts, local outbreaks, disease vectors (eg, mosquitoes, ticks), a common vehicle (eg, food, water), or geographic location (eg, residence in or recent travel to an endemic area).
